title: Domain Coverage: From the Planning Model to the Book's Chapters
basis: Written on 2026-11-17 from the page's PLAN contract, the author's planning model (29 capability bricks counted from its bricks file) and the written chapters: each mapping was confirmed by opening the chapter and finding a section that treats the capability. Intent, acceptance criteria, thesis and role are copied unchanged from journal-spec.json. A lookup page: tables are recorded as the evidence of the paragraph that introduces them.

know: Which chapter covers each of the 29 capability bricks of the Productscape model of payments and revenue infrastructure, in its four groups: merchant payments, revenue automation, platform money movement, shared financial foundations.

Which capabilities the book covers only briefly (for example hosted checkout and payment links as products, identity verification as a standalone product, delegated authority for agents) or leaves to sibling books, and why.

What the book added that the model has no brick for: how a card payment clears and settles, payment economics, acquiring and licenses, tokenization and PCI scope, authentication, idempotency, API versioning, the whole of Part VIII on scale, the journeys, the failure patterns and the company cases.

That the model is the author's planning map, built with Stripe as the modeled product and Adyen as the comparison, with logical records inferred from modeled jobs: never a source for a fact about either company.
can_do: Find the chapter for a system they own by the job it does.
Say whether a subject is absent from the book by decision or covered under another name.

Any three of: clearing and settlement, payment economics, acquiring and licenses, tokenization and PCI scope, network tokens, 3-D Secure and SCA, idempotency, API versioning, reliability, data stores, multi-region operation, peak load, safe change, the four journeys, the failure patterns, the Stripe and Adyen cases.

thesis.question: Which planning model stands behind the book, which chapters cover its capabilities, and what did the book cover briefly, leave out or add?
thesis.claim: The book was planned against a 29-capability Productscape model of payments and revenue infrastructure and gives every capability group at least one chapter, but it is organized differently from the model. It treats product-shaped capabilities (hosted checkout, payment links, standalone identity verification, delegated authority for agents) briefly, inside chapters about the mechanism beneath them; it leaves the finance-side posting of payouts to the sibling book RECONCILED; and it adds what the model has no capability for: how money moves between the parties, the mechanisms that make a retried or changed API call safe (idempotency, versioning, tokenization, authentication) and how the whole is run at scale. The model is a planning map and is evidence about no company.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a book planned from a capability model should follow that model chapter for chapter, so that a mismatch between the two is a gap in the book, and that a detailed model of Stripe's and Adyen's products can be cited for how those companies work.
thesis.so_what: A reader who owns a system finds its chapter by the job the system does, reads an absence as either a stated decision or a different name, and never quotes the model, or this page, for a fact about a provider.
thesis.how_why: A product model answers what a customer can buy and which job it does; an engineer new to payments first needs what happens to the money and why the obvious integration fails, which no product brick states. So Parts I, IV and VIII have few or no bricks behind them, while product-shaped bricks such as hosted checkout or payment links fold into chapters about the mechanism beneath them. The model's own description says it does not attempt to describe either company's internal service topology, physical databases or cloud regions, which is why it can guide coverage and cannot support a claim.

supporting_claims.claim: The planning model is a product and capability map of 29 bricks in four groups that describes no company's internal systems, so it guides coverage and is never a source for a fact.
Every one of the 29 capabilities is sent to the chapters that treat it, with a grade, and every capability group has at least one chapter of its own.
The capabilities the book treats in less than a chapter, and the parts of capabilities it leaves to sibling books, are named with the reason for each.
The ten subjects the author set out to cover each have chapters, and that list, not the model, explains the book's order.

The book adds what a product model has no capability for: how money moves between the parties, the mechanisms that make a retried or changed call safe, running the whole at scale, the journeys, the failure patterns and the company cases.

role.contribution: Opens the reference part and sends a reader from a capability to its chapter, saying plainly what is covered briefly, left out or added, and that the planning model is not evidence.

flow.rationale: What the model is comes first, because every table after it is read under the rule that the model is a map and not evidence. The whole map by capability follows, then the narrower questions a reader brings to it in turn: which capabilities get less than a chapter, whether the ten subjects the book set out to cover are all there, what the book added that the model lacks, and where a reader in a given seat should start. The added subjects come after the author's list because the list is the reason for most of them; putting the gaps before the map would list exceptions to a map the reader has not seen.

hook.content: The planning model behind this book, last reviewed on 15 November 2026, lists 29 capabilities of payments and revenue infrastructure in four groups. None of the 29 is named for card clearing, a card vault, 3-D Secure, idempotency or API versioning, and this book gives each of those a chapter.

conclusion.heading: One Map, Three Answers
conclusion.synthesis: The tables give three different answers to one lookup: a chapter (the capability is a mechanism the book teaches), a section or a mention (it is a product surface on top of one), or another book (it belongs to the finance, commerce or agent side). The pattern across them is that the book is organized by what happens to the money and the model by what can be bought.
conclusion.so_what: A reader who looks a system up by the job it does knows, before relying on the book, whether the answer is a chapter, a paragraph or elsewhere, and does not quote the model or this page for a fact about a provider.

takeaway.content: Match each system you own by the job it does, read the grade before the chapter, check the left-out list against your business, and treat the model as a map only; then continue to the toolkit.

open_questions: Flow rubric notes not acted on (the author decides): move p13 (the six stress scenarios) into the brief and left-out section, since it reports coverage and one gap rather than an addition; merge p15 (the engineer's question) into the conclusion's synthesis; let p07 only tally and leave the reason for briefer treatment to p09.

decision_log.decision: Four grades (chapter, section, mention, not covered), set by opening each chapter and finding a section that treats the capability. A paragraph or a table row inside a section on a wider subject counts as a mention, so hosted checkout (one of four ways to collect a card in tokenization-vaulting-and-pci) is graded mention, not section.
rejected: Grading from the PLAN contracts, which would grade what was promised and not what was written.
ORDERED's five labels (covered, covered briefly, mentioned only, thin, left out), which mix a grade with a reason.

decision_log.decision: One row per brick, in the model's group order, with the model's four-letter key kept so the count of 29 can be checked on the page.
rejected: Merging bricks into topic rows grouped by the book's parts, as ORDERED's page does for 152 capabilities; with 29 a row per brick is short enough and makes every number checkable.

decision_log.decision: The author's ten-subject list is a section after the gaps and before the added subjects, because the list is the cause of most additions.
rejected: Placing it first, which would put the book's own list before the model the page is named for.

decision_log.decision: No illustration: the style guide gives reference pages none, and the page is tables.
The model is described as the author's own unpublished planning input and named without a path or link; companies on its comparison list are named only to say which have a chapter.
rejected: Listing the model's path under Sources, as ORDERED's page does.
